title: ISO 9001:2015
source: ISO 9001:2015, clauses 4 to 10 (reference numbers and official short titles)
licence: Reference numbers with the official short titles only; not the text of the standard. Purpose, guidance, audit questions and typical evidence are our own words. Buy the standard for the requirements.

requirements.title: Clause 4 · Context of the organisation
requirements.purpose: Sets the foundation: what shapes the business, who cares about it and what the quality system covers.

requirements.title: Understanding the organization and its context
requirements.purpose: Makes sure the business knows the outside and inside factors that affect its ability to deliver quality results.
requirements.guidance: Hold a short, honest session with senior people and list the factors that matter: market, regulation, technology, suppliers, finances, culture, skills. Record them in a simple register with an owner and a review date, and link the important ones to your risks and objectives. A frequent finding is a one-off SWOT done for the first audit and never revisited. Auditors want to see the list change when the business does, for example after a new product, a lost customer or a regulatory change.
questions: How did you identify the factors that affect your ability to meet customer needs?
When did you last review these issues and what changed?
Which of these issues fed into your risk assessment or objectives?
How do you learn about changes in regulation or the market?
evidence: Context register or analysis with owner and review date
Minutes of the meeting where issues were discussed
Link from context items to risks or objectives

requirements.title: Understanding the needs and expectations of interested parties
requirements.purpose: Identifies who has a stake in the business and which of their needs the quality system must take into account.
requirements.guidance: List customers, regulators, owners, employees, key suppliers, insurers and any others who can affect or be affected by what you do. For each, note what they require or expect and which of those needs you have chosen to treat as binding, such as contract terms or legal duties. Keep it short and review it at least yearly. A common weakness is a generic list of parties with no link to actual requirements or to how you monitor them.
questions: Who are your interested parties and how did you decide they are relevant?
Which of their requirements are legal or contractual obligations?
How do you hear about changes in what they need?
How does this analysis influence your planning?
evidence: Date and owner of the last review

requirements.title: Determining the scope of the quality management system
requirements.purpose: Draws a clear boundary around what the quality system covers so everyone knows what is in and out.
requirements.guidance: Write a scope statement naming the products and services, sites, and activities covered, taking account of your context and interested parties. If a requirement of the standard does not apply, for example design, state it and give a sound reason that does not undermine conformity of your products. Make the scope available as documented information and keep it consistent with your website, certificate wording and contracts. Pitfalls include excluding something you actually do, or a scope that lags behind new sites or services.
questions: What is covered by your quality system and what is excluded?
Why do you consider any requirement not applicable?
Does the scope match what you tell customers you do?
When was the scope last reviewed?
evidence: Scope statement approved by top management
List of sites and services in scope
Review record showing the scope is current

requirements.title: Quality management system and its processes
requirements.purpose: Ensures the business runs on defined, connected processes that are owned, measured and improved.
requirements.guidance: Identify your main processes, from sales through delivery and support, and show how they connect, using a simple process map. For each, define the inputs and outputs, owner, resources, controls and measures, and the risks that matter. Keep documentation proportionate: a one-page process description beats a long manual nobody reads. Auditors often find maps that do not match reality, processes without owners or measures, and no evidence that processes are reviewed.
questions: Show me your process map and how the processes interact.
Who owns this process and how do you know it is working?
What indicators do you track for it?
How do you update processes when the way of working changes?
evidence: Process descriptions with owner, inputs, outputs and measures
Records of process reviews or changes

requirements.title: Clause 5 · Leadership
requirements.purpose: Makes senior people personally accountable for the quality system rather than leaving it to a quality manager.

requirements.title: Leadership and commitment
requirements.purpose: Requires senior management to take real ownership of the quality system and its results.
requirements.guidance: This clause is judged by what leaders do, not what documents say. Auditors will talk to the top team, so each person should be able to explain the policy, the objectives and how quality is resourced and reviewed. Show leadership through decisions: budget approvals, attendance at reviews, following up actions. Pitfall: delegating everything to a quality manager and being unable to describe the system when asked.
questions: How does top management demonstrate it owns the quality system?
What decisions has leadership made recently to support quality?
How do you make sure the system fits the business direction?
evidence: Management review minutes showing leadership decisions
Budget or resource approvals for quality work

requirements.title: Leading the quality system
requirements.purpose: Spells out what leaders must do to steer the quality system and keep it effective.
requirements.guidance: Leaders should set direction through policy and objectives, make sure processes are integrated into daily business, and provide the people and resources needed. They should also promote a process and risk-based approach and encourage staff to contribute to improvement. Keep evidence simple: dated decisions, meeting minutes and visible messages. A typical gap is objectives that are set but never discussed again until the next audit.
questions: How are quality objectives aligned with business strategy?
How do leaders communicate why quality matters?
What resources were added or changed because of quality needs?
How do you support managers in their roles in the system?
evidence: Policy and objectives approved by leadership
Resource decisions linked to system needs
Staff briefings or town hall notes

requirements.title: Customer focus
requirements.purpose: Ensures leaders keep customer requirements, legal duties and customer satisfaction at the centre of decisions.
requirements.guidance: Show how the business learns what customers need, how requirements are met consistently and how risks to satisfaction are spotted early. Typical evidence includes complaint trends, on-time delivery, survey results and actions taken. Leaders should be able to say what the key customer risks are. Auditors often see data collected but not used, so make sure customer results reach management review and trigger action.
questions: How do you know what customers need and expect?
Which risks could reduce customer satisfaction and how are they managed?
How are legal and customer requirements identified and kept up to date?
What did you change recently because of customer feedback?
evidence: Customer satisfaction or delivery performance data
Register of applicable legal and customer requirements

requirements.title: Policy
requirements.purpose: Gives the organisation a clear, communicated statement of intent for quality that guides objectives.
requirements.guidance: Write a short policy that fits your business, commits to meeting requirements and to improving the system, and gives a frame for objectives. Approve it at top level, keep it controlled, and make sure staff can find it and say what it means for their job. Share it with interested parties where relevant. Common findings are copied generic wording, policies with no link to objectives, and staff who have never seen it.
questions: Where is the policy displayed and communicated?
How is it appropriate to your business purpose?
What do staff understand it to mean for their own work?
When was it last reviewed?
evidence: Evidence of communication, for example intranet, induction, noticeboard
Staff awareness checks or interview results

requirements.title: Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities
requirements.purpose: Ensures it is clear who is responsible for what in the system and who can make decisions.
requirements.guidance: Define roles for the key process owners and for system tasks such as reporting on performance, promoting customer focus and keeping the system sound during changes. Capture them in role descriptions, an organisation chart or a responsibility matrix, and make sure the people know. Check cover for absences. Pitfalls include roles that exist only on paper, unclear ownership of processes, and out of date charts after reorganisations.
questions: Who is responsible for each process and how do they know?
Who reports on system performance to top management?
How do you handle cover for key roles?
How are changes to responsibilities communicated?

requirements.title: Clause 6 · Planning
requirements.purpose: Turns risks, opportunities and ambitions into planned, owned actions before problems happen.

requirements.title: Actions to address risks and opportunities
requirements.purpose: Makes the business think ahead about what could go wrong or help, and plan proportionate action.
requirements.guidance: Use the context and interested party work to list risks and opportunities that could affect results or customer satisfaction. Assess them simply, for example likelihood and impact, decide what to do, and assign owners and dates. Plan how to build actions into processes and how to judge if they worked. The standard does not require a formal risk method, so choose something people will actually use. Auditors often find a risk register written once and never updated, or risks with no actions.
questions: How did you identify the risks and opportunities in your processes?
How do you decide which ones to act on?
Show an action you took and how you checked it worked.
How often is the register reviewed?
evidence: Risk and opportunity register with owners and dates
Review records or management review inputs

requirements.title: Quality objectives and planning to achieve them
requirements.purpose: Sets measurable goals for quality and a plan to reach them.
requirements.guidance: Choose a small number of objectives that support the policy and customer satisfaction, such as on-time delivery, defect rate or complaint response time. Make each measurable, give it an owner, a deadline and a plan for resources and checking progress. Track results regularly and review them in management meetings. Pitfalls include vague aims, objectives with no baseline or data, and no follow-up when targets are missed.
questions: What are your quality objectives and how are they measured?
Who is responsible for each and what is the plan?
How are you performing against them?
What happens when an objective is off track?
evidence: Objectives register with targets, owners and dates

requirements.title: Planning of changes
requirements.purpose: Ensures changes to the system are made deliberately, without harming consistency of results.
requirements.guidance: When you change a process, structure, system or site, consider why, what could go wrong, which resources are needed, and who is responsible. Use a simple change request or checklist and record the decision. Make sure documents and training are updated afterwards. Auditors find changes made informally, such as a new tool or supplier, with no thought to the effect on the quality system.
questions: How do you plan and approve changes that affect the system?
Give an example of a recent change and how its risks were considered.
How do you keep the system working during the change?
How are affected documents and people updated?

requirements.title: Clause 7 · Support
requirements.purpose: Covers the people, equipment, knowledge and records the system depends on to work day to day.

requirements.title: Resources
requirements.purpose: Makes sure the system is given the means it needs to operate and improve.
requirements.guidance: Resources are not only money. Consider people, equipment, systems, environment, measuring tools and knowledge, and both what you have and what you need to buy. Link resource decisions to objectives and risks, and show that management reviews resource needs. A common gap is no evidence that resource shortfalls are noticed and raised, such as overworked teams or ageing equipment.
questions: How do you decide what resources the system needs?
Give an example of a resource shortfall and what was done.
What constraints do you have on internal capability or external providers?
evidence: Purchase approvals linked to quality needs

requirements.title: Providing what the system needs
requirements.purpose: Confirms that the business has identified and provided what the system needs, with attention to limits.
requirements.guidance: Look at what exists in house and what must come from outside, and note where capacity or capability is a limit. Keep a brief record linking resource needs to processes and objectives. Review at least yearly and whenever demand changes. Pitfall: treating this clause as paperwork when the real evidence is decisions, such as hiring or replacing equipment, taken for quality reasons.
questions: What internal limits affect your ability to deliver?
What do you need from external providers?
How are resource needs reviewed?
evidence: Hiring or investment decisions with quality rationale

requirements.title: People
requirements.purpose: Ensures enough competent people are available to run the system and deliver the service.
requirements.guidance: Work out staffing needs for each process, including peaks and holidays, and check that numbers and skills match. Keep an organisation chart, a skills overview and a plan for gaps, with temps or contractors covered by the same expectations. Auditors often spot single points of failure and teams relying on one expert with no cover.
questions: How do you decide how many people each process needs?
What happens when someone key is absent?
How do you manage contractors and temporary staff?

requirements.title: Infrastructure
requirements.purpose: Keeps buildings, equipment, software and transport fit for the work they support.
requirements.guidance: Identify the infrastructure that affects product or service quality: premises, machines, IT systems, vehicles and communications. Plan maintenance or replacement based on risk, and record faults and repairs. For small firms, a simple asset list with service dates and an issue log is enough. Typical findings are missed maintenance, unknown equipment ownership and unsupported software.
questions: What infrastructure is critical to quality and how is it maintained?
Show me maintenance records for a key item.
How are breakdowns handled and learned from?

requirements.title: Environment for the operation of processes
requirements.purpose: Ensures the physical and social conditions of work do not harm the quality of outputs.
requirements.guidance: Consider factors such as temperature, cleanliness, noise, lighting, ergonomics, safe working and a respectful, low-stress workplace where they affect results. Decide what matters for your processes, define limits and check them. For office or service businesses this may be about workload, remote working set-up and culture. Pitfall: ignoring this clause as irrelevant without checking whether conditions affect output.
questions: Which environmental factors affect the quality of your work?
How do you monitor them?
What is done when conditions are not suitable?
evidence: Health and safety or workplace assessments

requirements.title: Monitoring and measuring resources
requirements.purpose: Gives confidence that measurements used to judge conformity are valid and traceable.
requirements.guidance: List every device or method used to prove products or services meet requirements, such as scales, gauges, test software or surveys. Where accuracy matters, calibrate or verify against traceable references at set intervals and keep results. Label status, protect from damage, and assess what was affected when something is found out of tolerance. Common issues are overdue calibrations and no follow-up on previous results.
questions: Which equipment gives you results you rely on for acceptance?
How do you know it is accurate?
What do you do if a device is found out of tolerance?
evidence: Equipment register with calibration due dates
Procedure for verification of software or methods

requirements.title: Organizational knowledge
requirements.purpose: Protects and uses the knowledge the business needs to deliver consistently.
requirements.guidance: Identify critical knowledge such as technical know-how, customer history, lessons learned and supplier insight, and decide how to hold it: documentation, mentoring, shared drives or training. Plan how knowledge is kept when people leave and how new knowledge is obtained from conferences, customers or experts. Pitfalls include know-how living in one head and lessons learned never being captured.
questions: What knowledge is essential and where is it held?
What happens to that knowledge when someone leaves?
How do you gain new knowledge when needs or trends change?

requirements.title: Competence
requirements.purpose: Ensures people doing work that affects quality are able to do it, based on education, training or experience.
requirements.guidance: Define the competence needed for each role, check it at hiring, and close gaps with training, coaching or supervision. Then evaluate whether the training worked. Keep records of qualifications, training and sign-off proportionate to risk. Auditors often find training delivered but not assessed for effectiveness, or role requirements that were never written.
questions: How do you decide what competence each role needs?
How do you check someone is competent?
Show how you evaluated a recent training.
How are gaps tracked and closed?

requirements.title: Awareness
requirements.purpose: Makes sure people know the policy, their contribution and the effect of not following requirements.
requirements.guidance: Staff should be able to say, in their own words, what the quality policy means for them, which objectives they influence and what happens if requirements are not met. Build this into induction, team talks and visible reminders. Auditors test it by asking staff directly, so a prepared answer is not the same as understanding. Include contractors who work under your control.
questions: What is the quality policy and how does your job affect it?
Which objectives relate to your work?
What are the consequences of not following procedures?

requirements.title: Communication
requirements.purpose: Plans what is communicated about the system, to whom, when and how, inside and outside the business.
requirements.guidance: Decide the topics, audiences, timing, methods and responsible people for important communication, such as performance results, changes, customer updates and supplier requirements. A simple communications matrix works well. Check that messages reach people and that feedback is possible. Pitfalls include relying on ad hoc emails and having no clear way to tell staff about changes in procedures.
questions: How do you decide what to communicate and to whom?
How do staff hear about system changes?
How is external communication, for example with customers, controlled?

requirements.title: Documented information
requirements.purpose: Sets expectations for the documents and records that support and prove the system.
requirements.guidance: Keep what the standard asks for plus what your business needs to be effective, and no more. Make documents easy to find, current and approved, and keep records legible and retrievable. Think about who uses them and in what format. Auditors usually see two problems: too much documentation nobody follows, or key records missing.
questions: How do you decide which documents and records you need?
Where can staff find the current version?
How are records kept and for how long?
evidence: Evidence of current versions in use

requirements.title: What must be documented
requirements.purpose: Defines the minimum documented information and allows more where the business benefits.
requirements.guidance: Check your system includes the documents and records the standard calls for, such as scope, policy, objectives and evidence of results, and add only what adds value for your size, complexity and staff competence. A table mapping requirements to your documents helps audits. Pitfall: copying a large template set that does not match how you really work.
questions: Which documents are required and which did you add yourself?
How do you decide the extent of documentation for a process?
Show me where requirement X is documented.
evidence: Documented information list or map to the standard

requirements.title: Creating and updating
requirements.purpose: Ensures documents are identifiable, in a suitable format and approved before use.
requirements.guidance: Give each document a title, owner, version and date, and use a consistent template and review route. Approve before release and keep a change history so people know what changed. Use media that suit users, such as short checklists or video. Auditors often find unsigned documents, missing version numbers and approvals done informally in email with nothing recorded.
questions: How are documents identified and approved?
Who reviews and signs off changes?
How do you know a document is still suitable?
evidence: Document headers with version, date and author

requirements.title: Control of documented information
requirements.purpose: Keeps documents and records available, protected and under control throughout their life.
requirements.guidance: Make sure the right version is accessible where work happens, restrict editing, protect against loss and misuse, and manage distribution, storage, retention and disposal. Mark external documents such as customer specifications and control them as well. Back up electronic records and test restores. Common failures are obsolete copies still in use, uncontrolled spreadsheets and records kept longer or shorter than needed.
questions: How do you prevent use of out of date documents?
How are access and changes controlled?
How long are records retained and how are they disposed of?
How are external documents handled?
evidence: Master document list with current versions

requirements.title: Clause 8 · Operation
requirements.purpose: Controls how work is planned, designed, bought, delivered and checked so customers get what was promised.

requirements.title: Operational planning and control
requirements.purpose: Ensures the processes that deliver products and services are planned, controlled and kept in step with requirements.
requirements.guidance: For each product or service, define requirements, acceptance criteria, process controls, resources and the records needed to show conformity. Control planned changes and review the effects of unplanned ones. Make sure outsourced processes are also under control. Pitfalls include relying on tacit knowledge, not retaining records that show work met criteria, and changes made on the shop floor with no review.
questions: How do you plan the delivery of a typical order or project?
What criteria must outputs meet and how is that checked?
How do you control changes that happen during delivery?
How are outsourced processes controlled?
evidence: Process or project plans and checklists

requirements.title: Requirements for products and services
requirements.purpose: Ensures the business understands what customers need, can meet it, and agrees changes clearly.
requirements.guidance: Set out how you communicate with customers before, during and after sale, how enquiries, orders, contracts and complaints are handled, and how you collect requirements, including legal and unstated ones. Before committing, check you can deliver what you promise and resolve differences. Keep records of reviews and changes and tell staff when requirements change. Typical findings are verbal orders without confirmation and contract reviews that are not recorded.
questions: How do you capture and confirm customer requirements?
How do you check you can deliver before accepting an order?
What happens when a customer changes their order?
How do you handle customer property and complaints?
evidence: Quotes, orders and contracts with review evidence

requirements.title: Design and development of products and services
requirements.purpose: Controls how new or changed products and services are created so they meet needs and can be delivered.
requirements.guidance: If you design anything, even bespoke solutions, define stages, inputs, reviews, verification and validation, responsibilities and how changes are handled. Record why decisions were made and keep evidence that outputs meet the inputs. Where you do not design, state and justify it in the scope. Pitfalls include unclear input requirements, reviews only held informally and design changes not authorised or traced.
questions: Walk me through a recent design project from brief to release.
How did you verify and validate the result?
How are design changes controlled?
What records show who approved what?
evidence: Design plan with stages and responsibilities

requirements.title: Control of externally provided processes, products and services
requirements.purpose: Ensures that what suppliers provide meets requirements and is controlled in proportion to the risk.
requirements.guidance: Decide criteria to select, evaluate and re-evaluate suppliers, and define the controls according to their impact on your output. Communicate requirements clearly in purchase orders and check goods or services on receipt. Keep an approved supplier list with performance records. Common findings are suppliers never evaluated after initial approval, vague purchasing requirements and no action on poor performance.
questions: How do you select and approve suppliers?
How do you monitor supplier performance?
How do you tell suppliers what you need?
What did you do about a poor performing supplier?
evidence: Approved supplier list with evaluation criteria

requirements.title: Production and service provision
requirements.purpose: Keeps delivery of products and services under controlled conditions that give consistent results.
requirements.guidance: Ensure information on what to deliver, suitable equipment, monitoring and competent people are in place. Handle identification, traceability, customer property, preservation and post-delivery duties such as warranty or support. Validate processes whose results cannot be fully checked afterwards. Manage changes in production or delivery. Typical pitfalls are missing traceability, unrecorded handling of customer property and no plan for post-delivery obligations.
questions: How do you make sure work is carried out under controlled conditions?
How do you identify and trace outputs?
How do you look after customer property?
What post-delivery activities do you provide?

requirements.title: Release of products and services
requirements.purpose: Ensures nothing reaches the customer until planned checks have been completed and recorded.
requirements.guidance: Define what must be verified before release, such as inspection, testing or sign-off, and who is authorised to release. Keep evidence of conformity and who approved it. Any exception needs customer or authorised agreement. Pitfalls include release based on habit, no record of who authorised and gaps when the usual checker is away.
questions: What checks occur before delivery or handover?
Who is authorised to release output?
How is evidence of conformity kept?
What happens if a check has not been completed?

requirements.title: Control of nonconforming outputs
requirements.purpose: Prevents defective outputs from being used or delivered by mistake and ensures they are dealt with.
requirements.guidance: Identify and segregate outputs that do not meet requirements, decide what to do, such as correct, scrap, re-deliver or accept with approval, and check corrected work. Tell customers where needed and keep a record of the issue, decision and who decided. Feed repeated issues into corrective action. Common findings are nonconformities fixed quietly with no record and no look at causes.
questions: How are nonconforming items identified and kept from use?
Who decides what happens to them?
How is rework re-checked?
How do you learn from recurring problems?

requirements.title: Clause 9 · Performance evaluation
requirements.purpose: Checks, with data, whether the system and the business are performing as intended.

requirements.title: Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation
requirements.purpose: Makes the business decide what to measure and use the data to judge performance and effectiveness.
requirements.guidance: Select a handful of useful indicators across processes, define how and when to collect them and when to analyse. Use them to see whether the system delivers results and where to act. Keep results as records. A common finding is lots of data collected but no analysis or decisions drawn from it.
questions: What do you monitor and why?
How often do you analyse results and who sees them?
What decisions came from the data?

requirements.title: What to monitor and measure
requirements.purpose: Defines what is monitored, the methods used, and when results are analysed and evaluated.
requirements.guidance: For each process or objective, record what is measured, how, how often, who does it and when the results are reviewed. Choose methods that give valid results, such as consistent sampling or defined formulae. Evaluate performance and effectiveness, not only collect numbers. Pitfalls include indicators nobody owns and changing methods so trends cannot be compared.
questions: Which measures matter most to the system?
How do you make sure measurements are valid?
How do you judge the effectiveness of the system?
evidence: Measurement plan with owner and frequency

requirements.title: Customer satisfaction
requirements.purpose: Checks whether customers feel their needs and expectations have been met.
requirements.guidance: Gather views by methods that fit your business: surveys, reviews, complaints, repeat orders, account meetings or compliments. Decide how you collect, review and act on the information, and avoid relying on one weak signal. Use trends over time. Auditors look for evidence that the information is analysed and acted on rather than filed.
questions: How do you find out whether customers are satisfied?
What did the latest results show?
What actions did you take as a result?
How do you follow up with unhappy customers?

requirements.title: Analysis and evaluation
requirements.purpose: Turns collected data into judgements about conformity, customer satisfaction, system performance and improvement needs.
requirements.guidance: Analyse data to consider whether products meet requirements, how satisfied customers are, how well planning worked, whether actions on risk were effective, how suppliers perform and whether the system needs improving. Present it simply with trends and comparisons. Feed conclusions into management review. Pitfall: reports that describe numbers but never state what they mean or what to do.
questions: Show how you analyse your data to find trends.
What conclusions did you draw about supplier performance?
How did analysis lead to improvement?

requirements.title: Internal audit
requirements.purpose: Provides regular, impartial checks that the system conforms to requirements and is effectively implemented.
requirements.guidance: Create an audit programme that covers all processes and clauses over a cycle, weighting by importance and past results. Use auditors who are competent and not auditing their own work, define criteria and scope, report findings to relevant managers and follow up corrections. For a small company, a trained colleague from another team or an external auditor works. Pitfalls: audits that only tick boxes, findings with no follow-up and auditing own work.
questions: Show me your audit programme and how you set it.
How do you make sure auditors are impartial?
What did the last audit find and what happened next?
How do audit results feed management review?

requirements.title: Management review
requirements.purpose: Makes top management step back regularly to judge whether the system is suitable, adequate and effective.
requirements.guidance: Hold reviews at planned intervals, often once or twice a year, with the right people. Use a standing agenda to cover required inputs and record decisions, owners and dates. Follow up actions at the next meeting. Typical findings are reviews that only note information, missing inputs such as audit results or supplier performance, and no resource or improvement decisions.
questions: How often is management review held and who attends?
What inputs did you consider last time?
What decisions and actions came out?
How were actions followed up?

requirements.title: Reviews at planned intervals
requirements.purpose: Requires top management to review the quality system at planned intervals to keep it aligned with direction.
requirements.guidance: Plan the review dates in advance and treat them as a decision meeting, not a status report. Include top management in person and invite process owners who can contribute. Check alignment with strategy and context changes. Pitfall: a single annual meeting held days before the audit with prepared minutes.
questions: When are reviews scheduled and who must attend?
How does the review link to business strategy?
What happened if a planned review was missed?

requirements.title: Management review inputs
requirements.purpose: Defines the information that must be brought to the review so decisions are well informed.
requirements.guidance: Prepare a pack covering the status of previous actions, changes to issues and interested parties, performance and effectiveness data, adequacy of resources, effectiveness of risk actions and improvement opportunities. Performance data should include customer satisfaction, objectives, process results, nonconformities, monitoring results, audits and supplier performance. A checklist avoids gaps. Auditors often find several inputs absent.
questions: Show me the inputs you used in the last review.
How did you cover customer feedback and audit results?
How did you assess resource adequacy?

requirements.title: Management review outputs
requirements.purpose: Ensures reviews end in recorded decisions on improvement, system changes and resources.
requirements.guidance: Record conclusions on whether the system is suitable and effective, opportunities for improvement, any need for change and the resources required. Each decision should have an owner and date, be added to an action list and be followed up. Keep minutes as evidence. Pitfall: minutes that record discussion but no decisions, or decisions that disappear afterwards.
questions: What decisions did the last review make?
Who owns the resulting actions and are they complete?
Did the review change resources or objectives?

requirements.title: Clause 10 · Improvement
requirements.purpose: Ensures problems are fixed at the root and the system keeps getting better.

requirements.title: Finding ways to improve
requirements.purpose: Requires the business to look for and act on opportunities to improve products, services and the system.
requirements.guidance: Use inputs such as audit results, customer feedback, data analysis and management review to pick improvements that increase satisfaction, correct and prevent unwanted effects and improve performance. Keep a simple improvement log with owners and outcomes. Auditors like to see small, real changes that came from data rather than generic statements.
questions: What improvements have you made recently?
How do you choose which improvements to pursue?
How do you know they worked?

requirements.title: Nonconformity and corrective action
requirements.purpose: Ensures problems are contained, root causes found and fixes checked so they do not return.
requirements.guidance: When something goes wrong, from a complaint or audit finding, react to control and correct it, work out the cause, check whether it could happen elsewhere, act, and review whether the action worked. Match effort to impact. Record the nonconformity, actions and results. Frequent findings are fixes that treat the symptom only, no effectiveness check and actions closed late without evidence.
questions: Walk me through a recent corrective action.
How did you determine the root cause?
How did you check it was effective?
Do you look for similar issues elsewhere?
evidence: Updates to risks or documents after actions

requirements.title: Continual improvement
requirements.purpose: Commits the business to keep improving the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the system.
requirements.guidance: Use the outputs of analysis, evaluation and management review to identify needs or opportunities, and act on them. Show a trend of better results over time, for example fewer complaints or faster delivery. Make improvement part of normal management meetings, not only an audit preparation task. Pitfall: stating commitment without evidence of any measured gain.
questions: How do you drive continual improvement?
Show me results that have improved over time.
How do analysis and management review feed this?
